question: What did you say in your first address at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago?

result.text: I spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, where I expressed my gratitude for the warm and cordial welcome given to me and my fellow representatives.[1] I thanked the audience in the name of the most ancient order of monks in the world, the mother of religions, and millions of Hindu people of all classes and sects.[1] I emphasized the importance of representing Hinduism in a way that was clear, correct, and authoritative, which impressed the audience and led many to appreciate the spiritual depth of Indian traditions.[2] I called attention to the Hindu doctrine of the Harmony and Brotherhood of Religions, highlighting that all religions are part of a journey toward the same goal.[2] I stated that no faith or philosophy can survive to the exclusion of others, and that Truth and Holiness belong to all humanity.[2] I quoted from the Bhagavad-Gita, saying that the whole world of religions is a coming up of different men and women through various conditions to the same goal.[2]

question: How did your view of Buddhism relate to Hinduism in your Chicago addresses?

result.text: As I told the audience at the Parliament of Religions, I am not a Buddhist, as you have heard, and yet I am.[1] I explained that the relation between Hinduism and modern Buddhism is nearly the same as between Judaism and Christianity.[1] I stated that Shâkya Muni came not to destroy, but to fulfil and not to destroy the teachings of the Hindu religion.[1] I emphasized that the real difference between modern Buddhism and the teachings of Lord Buddha lies in the fact that his own followers did not realise the import of his teachings.[1] I noted that the Jews rejected Jesus Christ, while the Hindus have accepted Shâkya Muni as God and worship him.[1] I argued that the Buddhist command could only be carried out through monasticism, while Hinduism might be fulfilled through any state of life.[2] I pointed out that Hinduism never presumed to enunciate any rigid law for the realisation of the Real, unlike Buddhism.[2]

question: What did you write to Alasinga about starting work in Madras?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from the U. S. a in 1894 that I had done a good deal of work that year and hoped to do more in the next.[1] I told Alasinga that I did not believe in duty, but rather in truth, and that the universe was my country.[1] I encouraged Alasinga to work with determination and to have iron wills and hearts that do not know how to quake.[1] I wrote to Alasinga from the U. S. a in 1894 that I had done more for India than India ever did for me.[1] I told Alasinga that I sought no praise from India or America, but had a truth to teach.[1] I wrote to Alasinga from the U. S. a in 1894 that I believed in truth, and that the Lord would send me fellow workers from the earth's bravest and best.[1]

question: What did you say about the condition of the masses in India?

result.text: As I spoke at the lecture on My Life and Mission, I described India as an enslaved race with no say in its own government, where three hundred millions of people are slaves, and the average income is two shillings a month.[1] In a conversation with Shri Priya Nath Sinha, I noted that the masses have lost their manliness and become like professional beggars, while the highly-educated clamour for more from the English rulers.[2] I remarked in an interview that our masses are very good because poverty here is not a crime, and they are not violent, unlike in America and England.[3] In an interview, I stated that the great national sin is the neglect of the masses, and that no amount of politics would help India until the masses are well educated, fed, and cared for.[4] I described the masses as three hundred million souls crushed out of life by being downtrodden by their own people and foreign nations, devoid of initiative and full of diabolical superstitions.[5] I emphasized that India wants not lecturing but work, and that the crying problem in India is poverty, urging young sannyasins to be trained as secular and spiritual teachers for the masses.[6]

question: What was your position on the caste system?

result.text: I argued that the caste system is a social custom, not a religious institution, and that all our great preachers have tried to break it down.[1] I stated that caste is simply the outgrowth of the political institutions of India; it is a hereditary trade guild.[1] I explained that the caste system has nothing to do with religion, and that a man's occupation is hereditary.[2] I acknowledged that the caste system is a very good thing, and that it is the plan we want to follow.[3] I said that caste is based throughout on the principle of making everybody a Brahmin, the Brahmin being the ideal of humanity.[3] I noted that the caste system has grown by the practice of the son always following the business of the father, and that it has united the people by binding them to help their fellows in case of need.[4] I emphasized that the caste system is not a granted system of classes, but that each caste thought itself to be superior to all the others.[5] I stated that the caste system is a hereditary caste system, and that the improvement of the lower classes of India will go on so long as India will be under a government dealing with its subjects irrespective of their caste and position.[6]

question: What did you say about the education of women in India?

result.text: I argued that our right of interference is limited entirely to giving education, and women must be put in a position to solve their own problems in their own way.[1] I stated that our Indian women are as capable of solving their own problems as any in the world.[1] I questioned what sort of education is suited to our women, emphasizing the need for education that aligns with our national lines and religious ordinances.[2] I pointed out that only three or four per cent of the people in India are educated, and not even one per cent of the women.[3] I noted that in modern times there is a greater impetus towards higher education on European lines, and the trend of opinion is strong towards women getting this higher education.[4] I emphasized that our religion does not prevent a woman being educated at all, and that the girl should be educated in the spirit of our own religious ordinances.[4] I stressed that the uplift of the women and the awakening of the masses must come first, and then only can any real good come about for the country, for India.[5] I explained that female education is to be spread with religion as its centre, and that all other training should be secondary to religion.[6]

question: How did you describe your Master, Shri Ramakrishna, in your lectures?

result.text: I described my Master, Shri Ramakrishna, as a great soul whose teachings have spread beyond India and whose influence is felt worldwide.[1] I told the audience that the power of Shri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa is known all over India to its millions of people.[1] I emphasized that I owe all the spiritual truths I have spoken anywhere in the world to my Master, though I acknowledge my own mistakes.[1] I recounted how my Master, Shri Ramakrishna, refused to use his mental power for his own healing, instead dedicating his mind entirely to God.[2] I described my Master as one who had discovered the wonderful unity underlying everything, experienced it in Hinduism, Islam, and Christianity.[3] I mentioned that my Master had given us the desire and the lifelong struggle to live the life, not just to talk about it.[4] I told the audience that Shri Ramakrishna had left us with a great gift, the desire to live the life and not just talk about it.[4]

question: What did you tell the people of Madras when you returned from the West?

result.text: I offered the people of Madras a most hearty welcome on the occasion of my return from my Religious Mission in the West.[1] I expressed my feelings of joy and pleasure on my safe return to India and offered my heartfelt congratulation on the great success which had attended my unselfish efforts in Western lands.[2] I told them that the contradictions of the world's numerous creeds are all reconciled in the universal light of the Vedanta.[2] I declared that all the peoples of the world have need to understand and practically realise the great truth that 'Unity in variety' is nature's plan in the evolution of the universe.[2] I expressed the hope that under my high and holy auspices, we of the present generation would witness the inauguration of a new era in the world's history, in which bigotry, hatred, and conflict may cease, and peace, sympathy, and love reign among men.[2] I told them that the Western world has come to understand what an inexhaustible store of spirituality India has even today.[2] I told them that the contradictions of the world's numerous creeds are all reconciled in the universal light of the Vedanta.[2]

question: What did you say about idol worship when questioned in the West?

result.text: I was asked about idol worship in the West, and I explained that all forms of worship, including idol worship, are stages in the spiritual journey.[1] I clarified that idol worship is not the highest form of devotion, but it is a necessary stage for many people in their spiritual development.[1] I emphasized that the worship of an idol is not the same as worshipping God Himself, and that one must eventually transcend the image to see the divine.[1] I noted that even in the West, people may express their devotion in various ways, and that no single form of worship is superior to others.[1] I acknowledged that some may view idol worship as a form of idolatry, but I argued that it is a means to an end, helping individuals progress spiritually.[1] I stated that the same earnest man who kneels before an idol can also speak of a God beyond all forms, showing that idol worship is a stepping stone to higher realization.[2] I pointed out that even in the West, people may worship in a personal form, which could be seen as a type of idol worship in another sense.[3] I argued that idol worship is not inherently wrong, and that people should be helped to move beyond it if they are able, rather than being judged harshly for their current stage.[3]

question: What did you write about the relationship between science and religion?

result.text: I wrote that science is nothing but the finding of unity, and as soon as science would reach perfect unity, it would stop from further progress, because it would reach the goal.[1] I explained that just as chemistry would stop when it discovers one element from which all others are derived, so too would the science of religion become perfect when it discovers the one life in a universe of death.[1] I noted that all science has its particular methods, and so does the science of religion, which has more methods because it has more material to work upon.[2] I emphasized that the human mind is not homogeneous like the external world, and according to the different nature, there must be different methods in the science of religion.[2] I pointed out that experience is the only source of knowledge, and in the world, religion is the only science where there is no surety, because it is not taught as a science of experience.[3] I stated that the real science of religion is based on the experience of mystics, who in every religion speak the same tongue and teach the same truth.[3] I argued that every science must end where it finds a unity, because we cannot go any further, and when a perfect unity is reached, that science has nothing more of principles to tell us.[4]

question: What did you say about Christ in your lecture 'Christ, the Messenger'?

result.text: I argued that God is not only found in Jesus of Nazareth but also in all the great Ones who have preceded him and those who come after him.[1] I emphasized that our worship is unbounded and free, as all these great Ones are manifestations of the same Infinite God.[1] I stated that they all struggled and gave up their lives for us, poor human beings, and that they each suffer vicarious atonement for every one of us and for all that are yet to come.[1] I explained that the life of Christ is the life of all the past, and that every man's life is, in a manner, the life of the past, coming to him through heredity, surroundings, education, and reincarnation.[2] I said that we are but a result of the infinite past, floating waveless in the eternal current of events, irresistibly moved forward and incapable of rest.[2] I pointed out that the past of the earth, the past of the whole world is upon every soul, and that we are but little things, bubbles in the ocean of affairs.[2] I noted that there are always some giant waves in the ocean of affairs, and that there are giants who embody, as it were, almost the whole of the past and who stretch out their hands for the future.[2] I stated that these are the sign-posts here and there which point to the march of humanity, and that they are verily gigantic, their shadows covering the earth — they stand undying, eternal![2]

question: What did you say about Mohammedanism and Islam?

result.text: I spoke about Mohammedanism in the lecture on the way to the realisation of a universal religion, where I noted that all old religions, including Mohammedanism, have kept their mission intact despite their mistakes and difficulties.[1] I pointed out that Mohammedanism, despite its sensual ideas in some parts of the Koran, preaches practical brotherhood of all its followers, which is its essential part.[1] I mentioned that in many places in the Koran, there are very sensual ideas of life, but I said never mind, as the essential part of Mohammedanism is the practical brotherhood of all belonging to their faith.[1] I noted that in the United States, I have never seen a church where the white man and the negro can kneel side by side to pray, unlike in Islam, where followers are all equal.[1] In a letter to Akhandananda, I said that Mohammedan boys must be admitted, but their religion should not be tampered with, and they should be taught to be moral and devoted to doing good to others.[2] In a lecture on the great teachers of the world, I said that Mohammed was the Messenger of equality, and that there should be perfect equality and brotherhood among Mohammedans, regardless of race, caste, creed, colour, or sex.[3] I noted that the Sultan of Turkey would have no objection to dine with a Mohammedan American Indian, showing the equality and brotherhood that Islam promotes.[1]

question: What were your views on the Vedas and their authority?

result.text: I argued that the Vedas are not the utterance of any person, but eternal knowledge that has always existed.[1] I stated that the Vedas do not owe their authority to any personal being, but are themselves the authority, being eternal knowledge of God.[1] I explained that the Vedas were never written or created, but have existed throughout time, just as creation is infinite and eternal.[1] I emphasized that the authority of the Vedas extends to all ages, climes, and persons, meaning their application is not confined to any particular place, time, or person.[2] I acknowledged that only those portions of the Vedas which agree with reason should be accepted as authority, while other Shâstras should be accepted only so far as they do not go against the Vedas.[3] I clarified that the correct meaning of the statement 'The Vedas are beginningless and eternal' is that the law or truth revealed by them to man is permanent and changeless.[4] I stated that the Vedas are the eternal knowledge through which God created the world, and they talk high philosophy — the highest — and make this tremendous claim.[5] I noted that the Vedas are a sort of incarnation of universal knowledge, and they have come out of Brahman as a man breathes out air, showing that He is infinite in power and knowledge.[6]

question: What did you say about the Sikhs and Guru Govind Singh?

result.text: I spoke of Guru Govind Singh during a conversation at Balaram Babu's residence, where I recounted his life and the revival of the Sikh sect through his renunciation and austerities.[1] I emphasized that Guru Govind Singh united Hindus and Muslims under his religion, a rare example in Indian history, as no other figure had done so.[2] I noted that Guru Govind Singh did not create a common interest but pointed out the injustice and oppression of his time, which led both Hindus and Muslims to follow him.[3] I quoted a Sikh Dohâ that illustrates the power infused into initiates by Guru Govind Singh, showing how one man could triumph over many foes.[4] In my lecture on the Common Bases of Hinduism, I praised Guru Govind Singh as an example of love and sacrifice, even when deserted by those for whom he had fought.[5] I highlighted that Guru Govind Singh's spiritual work led to the political organization of the Sikhs, showing how spiritual upheaval often precedes political unity.[6] I mentioned that Guru Govind Singh was a great worshipper of Shakti, and his ability to unite people despite his religious devotion was a rare example in Indian history.[3]

question: What did you write to Sister Nivedita about her work for Indian women?

result.text: I wrote to Sister Nivedita from The Math on April 4, 1901, expressing my gladness to learn of her good work in England and joining in earnest prayer with the hopes I had for her future services to India by her pen.[1] I also wrote to Sister Nivedita from The Math on April 4, 1901, telling her that she could stay as long as she thought she was working well.[2] In a letter to Sister Nivedita from Gopal Lal Villa on March 4, 1902, I mentioned that I had sent Christina Greenstidel £100 from Mrs. Sevier for a travel to India, as she had lost her mother at that time.[3] I also wrote to Sister Nivedita from Gopal Lal Villa on March 4, 1902, asking her to open Christina's letters directed to me, receive the girl, and send her back home if she had no money to go back.[3]

question: What did you say about vegetarianism and meat-eating?

result.text: I wrote in 'The East and the West' that to eat meat is surely barbarous and vegetable food is certainly purer — who can deny that?[1] I argued that for him surely is a strict vegetarian diet whose one end is to lead solely a spiritual life.[1] I stated that he who has to steer the boat of his life with strenuous labour through the constant life-and-death struggles and the competition of this world must of necessity take meat.[1] I explained that so long as there will be in human society such a thing as the triumph of the strong over the weak, animal food is required; otherwise, the weak will naturally be crushed under the feet of the strong.[1] I taught meat-eating throughout the length and breadth of India in the hope that we can build a militant spirit.[2] I noted that in the West, the contention is whether animal food is injurious to health or not, whether it is more strengthening than vegetable diet or not, and so on.[3] They do not take meat, but live somehow on the scanty diet of rice and all sorts of vegetables.'[3]

question: What was your opinion of social reformers in India?

result.text: Most of them are good, well-meaning men, and their aims too are very laudable on certain points.[1] I have nothing to do directly with your castes or with your social reformation.[1] Platform speeches have been made by the thousand, denunciations in volumes after volumes have been hurled upon the devoted head of the Hindu race and its civilisation, and yet no good practical result has been achieved.[1] It is in the denunciation itself.[1] I am sorry to say that most of our modern reform movements have been inconsiderate imitations of Western means and methods of work; and that surely will not do for India.[1] There is infinite power of development in everything; that is my belief.[2] All the modern reformers take to European destructive reformation, which will never do good to anyone and never did.[2]

question: What did you say about the Theosophists?

result.text: I wrote to my brave boys that the Theosophical magazines claiming they prepared the way to my success were pure nonsense.[1] In my essay on Theosophy, I noted that the Theosophists claim to possess the original divine knowledge of the universe, which we are glad they mean to keep a secret.[2] I remarked that in India, Theosophists and Buddhists are nonentities, merely publishing papers and trying to catch Occidental ears.[3] I wrote to Alasinga that the Theosophists here like me, but they are 650 in all, and I work with them but do not join any.[4] I observed that the Theosophists are having a jubilee time of it this year, with several press-notices of their activities over the past twenty-five years.[5] I stated that the Theosophists have not much power, but they are dead set against the orthodox section.[6] I wrote that the only help the religion of the Hindus got from the Theosophists was years of uphill work, necessitated by their sleight-of-hand methods.[7]

question: What did you say about the English and British rule in India?

result.text: I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor that despite the centuries of anarchy and the terrible massacre in 1857 and 1858, there has been a good increase of population in India under British rule, though not yet what it was when the country was entirely independent.[1] I noted that Indian labour and produce can support five times as many people as there are now in India with comfort, if the whole thing is not taken off from them.[1] I observed that the English public is forming the idea that the passing away of the Indian Empire from their sway will end in imminent peril to the English nation, and be their ruin, so they must maintain their supremacy in India.[2] I remarked that the English are trying to maintain their prestige and glory in India, but I argued that it is useless to spend so much energy for the mere preservation of meaningless 'prestige' when that power could be used for the welfare of the subject-people.[2] I wrote that the English have brought India out once more on the stage of the world, forcing upon it the contact of the outside world, though it could have been more wonderful for India if it had been done with an eye to the good of the people.[3] I stated that the English rule has only one redeeming feature, though unconscious; it has brought India out once more on the stage of the world; it has forced upon it the contact of the outside world.[3] I noted that the English have changed the criminal law in India, but the civil law remains the same, and that the judges, however, were Englishmen who did not know the language of the country in which the civil laws were written, and so they had to take the help of interpreters, lawyers of India, and so on.[4]

question: What did you tell Mrs. Bull about your plans for the Math at Belur?

result.text: I wrote to Mrs. Bull from Murree on October 11, 1897, stating that she had given much of the money and had implicit confidence in Sharat.[1] I also told her to do the work of the Math with Sharat's advice or as she saw fit.[1] In a letter to Mrs. Alice Hansbrough from Benaras on February 14, 1902, I mentioned that all letters should be addressed to the Belur Math.[2] In a letter to Mrs. Ole Bull from Dacca on March 20, 1901, I informed her that Mrs. Sevier was the guest of Mrs. Banerjey at the old Math.[3] I also told her that Mrs. Sevier was going to Europe soon.[3] In a letter to Sister Christine from The Math on January 26, 1899, I mentioned that I was in the vale of death and had been suffering from a disease that gave me the sensation of suffocation.[4] I told her that I was in Calcutta for rest and quiet and that if I got well by March, I would start for Europe.[4]

question: What did you write about the historical evolution of India?

result.text: I wrote about the historical evolution of India, noting that the Vedas are the common source of Hinduism in all its varied stages, as well as of Buddhism and every other religious belief in India.[1] I explained that the seeds of the multifarious growth of Indian thought on religion lie buried in the Vedas, and that Buddhism and other religious thoughts are the outcome of the unfolding and expansion of those seeds.[1] I described how the ancient history of India is full of descriptions of the gigantic energies and their multifarious workings, the boundless spirit, and the profound thoughtfulness of a godly race.[2] I noted that the ancient remains at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, and other sites in the Indus Valley prove the existence of an advanced city civilisation in India dating back to more than 3000 B.C.[3] I wrote that the commerce of India is perhaps the most important of all the causes which have worked for the present state of human civilisation from ancient times, as India has beaten all other countries in point of fertility and commercial industries.[4] I mentioned that the northern reaction of ritualism was followed by the fitful glory of the Malava empire, and that the south experienced a spiritual upheaval led by Shankara and Ramanuja.[5] I stated that the law of causation is omnipotent and knows no time or place when it did not exist, a doctrine as old as the Aryan race, sung by its ancient poet-seers and formulated by its philosophers.[6]

question: How did you describe the Sannyasin's ideal in your poem?

result.text: I described the Sannyasin as one who has no home, with the sky as their roof and the grass as their bed, and who judges no food or drink as tainting the noble Self.[1] I urged the Sannyasin to let darkness go and to conquer the thirst for life, which drags the soul from birth to death and back again.[2] I called upon the Sannyasin to renounce all life, heavens, earths, hells, hopes, and fears, and to cut their bonds.[3] I asked the Sannyasin where they seek, and told them that this world cannot give the freedom they seek, and that their only hope lies in letting go of the rope that drags them on.[4] I told the Sannyasin that the Self is all in all, and that they are That, the sexless Self, who has no father, child, friend, or foe.[5] I encouraged the Sannyasin to go forth from place to place, helping others out of the darkness of Maya's veil, without fear of pain or search for pleasure.[6] I warned the Sannyasin that truth never comes where lust, fame, and greed reside, and that they must give these up to pass through Maya's gates.[7]

question: What did you say to your brother disciples about organising the Ramakrishna Mission?

result.text: I wrote to my brother disciples at Alambazar Monastery that I was giving them a new idea, and if they could work it out, I would know they were men and would be of service.[1] I told them to make an organised plan, and to gather a number of poor, indigent folk, then show them pictures to teach them astronomy, geography, and preach Shri Ramakrishna to them.[1] I urged them to go to the cottages of the poor and open their eyes through oral teaching, as books would not do.[1] I encouraged them to slowly extend their centres and asked if they could do all this or only bell-ringing.[1] I also wrote to my brother disciples that I had heard everything about Brother Tarak from Madras and that they were highly pleased with him.[2] I told them that if Brother Tarak went to Madras and lived there for some time, a lot of work would be done, but before that, he should start the work there first.[2] I asked if the lady devotees could convert some widows into disciples and put a bit of learning into their heads, then send them out to preach Sri Ramakrishna from door to door.[2]

question: What did you say about Shankaracharya and Advaita?

result.text: I spoke about Shankaracharya and Advaita in a lecture where I pointed out that even great commentators like Shankaracharya, Râmânujâchârya, and Madhvâchârya had committed mistakes in interpreting the Upanishads.[1] I explained that Shankaracharya mistakenly believed the whole of the Upanishads taught only Advaitism, and he twisted the meaning of passages that supported the Dvaita idea to fit his own theory.[1] I noted that the Upanishads had one thing to teach, but that was taught as a going up from one step to another, and the final evolution to Advaitism was the natural outcome.[1] I emphasized that the influence of Shankaracharya was immense in Southern India, and his disciples became the great preachers of Advaita both in Southern and Northern India.[2] I mentioned that Shankaracharya was one of the last representatives of the Advaita system, which had existed ages before he was born.[3] I stated that the real essence of Buddhism and that of the Vedanta are not very different, and Shankara showed that the disciples had degraded themselves and denied the existence of the soul and of God.[4] I remarked that Shankaracharya's writings are the wonders of the modern world, and he wanted to bring back the Indian world to its pristine purity.[4]

question: What did you say about Ramanuja and qualified non-dualism?

result.text: I explained that Ramanuja is the leading dualistic philosopher of later India, whom all the other dualistic sects have followed, directly or indirectly, both in the substance of their teaching and in the organization of their sects even down to some of the most minute points of their organization.[1] I noted that according to Ramanuja, these three entities are eternal — God, and soul, and nature.[2] I stated that the system of Ramanuja admits the unity of the total, within that totality of existence there are, according to him, eternal differences.[3] I emphasized that the qualified non-dualists express it more beautifully than the dualists, by saying that the soul's purity and perfection become contracted and again become manifest, and what we are now trying to do is to remanifest the intelligence, the purity, the power which is natural to the soul.[4] I mentioned that the qualified non-dualistic system includes the largest number of the Indian people, and that the non-dualists are comparatively few in number.[5] I explained that the qualified non-dualistic system includes the largest number of the Indian people, and that the non-dualists are comparatively few in number.[5]

question: What did you say about the Buddha as a person?

result.text: I said that Buddha stood head and shoulders above all other men.[1][2] I said that his friends or enemies could never say that he drew a breath or ate a crumb of bread but for the good of all.[1][2] I said that Buddha's message is a tremendous message that has a place in our heart.[3] I said that Buddha taught that root out selfishness, and everything that makes you selfish.[3] I said that Buddha was born for the good of men and that he sought truth because people were in misery.[4] I said that Buddha was the first human being to give to the world a complete system of morality.[5] I said that Buddha was more brave and sincere than any teacher.[5]

question: What did you say about the role of the Brahmin in India's future?

result.text: I argued that the Brahmin must work for the salvation of the rest of mankind in India, and if he does that, he remains a true Brahmin.[1] I stated that the Brahmin must open the treasury of virtue and distribute its valuables to the world, as he was the earliest preacher to the Indian races.[1] I emphasized that the Brahmin must not occupy himself with any secular business and must not receive gifts from everybody, as his life is one of continuous renunciation.[2] I pointed out that the Brahmin must give to the people at large the accumulated culture of ages, and it was because he did not do so that the Mohammedan invasion was possible.[3] I urged that the Brahmin must be the first to break open the cells that hide the wonderful treasures accumulated by our common ancestors and give them to everybody.[3] I said that the Brahmin must not be allowed to remain in his exclusive privileges and exclusive claims, as the days of such privileges are gone for ever from the soil of India.[1] I noted that the Brahmin must be the ideal of humanity in India, as wonderfully put forward by Shankaracharya, and that he must remain as the man of God.[4] I explained that the Brahmin must not be allowed to remain in his exclusive privileges and exclusive claims, as the days of such privileges are gone for ever from the soil of India.[1]

question: What did you say about American women?

result.text: I praised the American women most enthusiastically, highlighting their kindness and the role they play in the nation's progress.[1] I remarked on the absence of poverty in America and expressed a good impression of the country and its women.[2] I noted that American women have many privileges and are slowly taking over various roles, with a greater number of cultured women than cultured men.[3] I observed that American women are more advanced than their men, with the average woman being far more cultivated.[4] I stated that in America, women are the life of every movement and represent all the culture of the nation, as men are too busy to educate themselves.[1] I remarked that in America, women are more learned than men, and that they are well versed in science and philosophy.[5] I expressed gratitude for the kindness of American women and wished them blessings.[1]

question: What did you say about the Jains?

result.text: I spoke about the Jains in an interview, noting that they are the most tolerant of all races of men, despite their profound religious beliefs.[1] I described the Jains as a sect that shows remarkable kindness to dumb animals, with their moral law summed up in the words: 'Not to injure others is the highest good.'[2] In a lecture, I emphasized that the Jains were the first great ascetics who elaborated the principle of non-injury and doing good as the foundation of all morality and ethics.[3] I mentioned that the Jains were a conservative force in India, even today, and that they declared against the validity of the Hindu scriptures, claiming their own books were the original Vedas.[4] I noted that the Jains were a sect that believed in the soul but not in the moral government of the country, and that they had millions of followers in India.[5] I highlighted that the Jains still survive in India, with only about a million remaining, and that their survival is due to their books.[6] I mentioned that the Jains were a sect that believed in the soul but not in the moral government of the country, and that their priests and monks tied handkerchiefs over their faces to avoid harming others.[5]

question: What did you write about the Paris Congress of the History of Religions?

result.text: I wrote about the Paris Congress of the History of Religions, noting that it was attended only by scholars devoted to the study of the origin and history of different religions.[1] I described the Congress as being similar to the Congress of Orientalists, with European scholars versed in Oriental languages meeting there.[2] I mentioned that the Congress did not include discussions on the doctrines and spiritual views of any religion, focusing instead on the historic evolution of established faiths.[1] I noted that the Congress was not a big affair, with only twenty scholars discussing topics like the origin of the Shâlagrâma and Jehovah.[3] I stated that the substance of my lecture at the Congress would be printed in French in the General Report of the Congress.[4] I observed that the Roman Catholics, who had previously organised the Chicago Parliament of Religions, were now opposing any similar gathering in Paris.[1] I remarked that the Congress was not intended to be a platform for religious debate, but rather a scholarly inquiry into the history of religions.[1]

question: What did you say about the Vedanta being practical?

result.text: I have been asked to say something about the practical position of the Vedanta philosophy.[1] As I have told you, theory is very good indeed, but how are we to carry it into practice?[1] If it be absolutely impracticable, no theory is of any value whatever, except as intellectual gymnastics.[1] The Vedanta, therefore, as a religion must be intensely practical.[1] We must be able to carry it out in every part of our lives.[1] The ideals of religion must cover the whole field of life, they must enter into all our thoughts, and more and more into practice.[1] The Vedanta preaches the ideal; and the ideal, as we know, is always far ahead of the real, of the practical, as we may call it.[2] It is a great thing to understand this, for the former tendency is the temptation of our lives.[2] The Vedanta teaches men to have faith in themselves first.[2] The Vedanta also says that not only can this be realised in the depths of forests or caves, but by men in all possible conditions of life.[3]

question: What did you say about Kali and Mother worship?

result.text: I wrote to Swami Brahmananda from the U.S.A. on 1899-11-20 that I bless you all on this day sacred to the Divine Mother, and that the Mother will certainly come down with great strength to bring all victory, world victory.[1] I told the disciple at Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that the figure of Mother Kali represents the union of the blissful and the terrible aspects, though none of the pictures can adequately express these aspects.[2] I performed a Homa before the Mother Kali at Kalighat, and I was glad to see that there was yet a liberality of view at Kalighat, as the temple authorities did not object to my entering the temple.[3] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Los Angeles on 1900-06-17 that Kali worship is not a necessary step in any religion, and that the Upanishads teach us all there is of religion.[4] I said that I believe in Brahman and also in the multitude of gods, just as the body is made up of many cells producing consciousness.[5]

question: What did you say about the hymn 'As the different streams having their sources in different places'?

result.text: I will quote to you, brethren, a few lines from a hymn which I remember to have repeated from my earliest boyhood, which is every day repeated by millions and millions of human beings: 'As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.'[1] I feel that the very spirit of this hymn, which I remember to have repeated from my earliest boyhood, which is every day repeated by millions and millions of men in India, has at last come to be realized.[2] As the Vedantist says in his poetical language, 'As so many rivers, having their source in different mountains, roll down, crooked or straight, and at last come into the ocean — so, all these various creeds and religions, taking their start from different standpoints and running through crooked or straight courses, at last come unto THEE.'[3] Yet they all tell you they are but different manifestations of religion.[4] This is not a theory, it has to be recognised, but not in that patronising way which we see with some people: 'Oh yes, there are some very good things in it.'[4]

question: What did you say about the Gita and Krishna's historicity?

result.text: As I discussed in my lecture on the Gita, the book forms a part of the Mahâbhârata, and understanding it properly requires knowing whether it was originally part of the epic or interpolated later.[1] I noted that it is human nature to build imaginary superhuman attributes around great men, and while Krishna may have been a king, the Gita's teachings align with those of the Mahabharata, suggesting a great man preached Brahma-Jnâna in that era.[2] I pointed out that the style and language of the Gita are the same as the Mahabharata, and the doctrines of the Gita do not mention Buddhism, which is a significant coincidence.[3] I mentioned that Krishna is loved and worshipped similarly to Christ, and while I do not know if he ever lived, I believe there must have been a man called Krishna whose Gita reflects a wonderful book.[4] I acknowledged that the Gita harmonizes conflicting doctrines and that even if Krishna did not live, the Gita's teachings are a result of a great man's efforts to reconcile different paths.[5] I noted that the Gita is not Krishna's only sermon, and that the central idea of non-attachment in Krishna's life is reflected in the fables about him.[6] I wrote to Mr.__ that the Gita has become the Bible of Hinduism, but the personality of Krishna is so obscured that it is difficult to draw life-giving inspiration from it today.[7]

question: How did you define religion in your lectures?

result.text: I defined religion as the realisation of Spirit as Spirit, not Spirit as matter.[1] I explained that religion is the manifestation of the Divinity already in man.[2] I said that religion is not merely talk or doctrines, but being and becoming, not hearing or acknowledging.[3] I taught that religion is the realisation of the universal, where one sees God in every person and feels the oneness of all beings.[4] I argued that religion is not a matter of intellectual assent, but of transforming one's whole nature into the truth.[3] I stated that religion is the science of experience, where mystics in every religion speak the same truth.[5] I said that religion is not a political something or a mass of superstition, but the realisation of the same God answering all.[6] I explained that religion is the only science where there is no surety, because it is not taught as a science of experience, but mystics teach it from experience.[5]

question: What did you say about the problem of evil?

result.text: As I discussed in my lecture on 'Worshipper and Worshipped', the problem of evil arises because if God is only good, then evil must be something else, which leads to contradictions.[1] I argued that good and evil are not separate existences, but part of an evolving process where what is less good is called evil.[2] I stated that the existence of evil is not something we need to explain, but rather something we must accept with faith and remain silent about.[3] I explained that temporal pain and sorrow, if they contribute to nobility and tenderness, may be considered supreme good rather than evil.[4] I noted that evil is a part of the world, and that even good things can become evil if taken to excess, such as drinking wine.[5] I emphasized that the view of absolute separation between good and evil leads to jealousy and hatred, which is more evil than evil itself.[2] I acknowledged that people often try to deny or forget evil, but this is a weakness that stems from fear.[3] I suggested that we must face facts as they are, without being chased by the idea of evil, and simply accept that evils are evils.[6]

question: What did you say about hypnotism and psychic powers?

result.text: I wrote to Shri Priya Nath Sinha that I have heard that their spiritual and psychic powers are very quickly developed when they practice religion.[1] I told the audience at the Graduate Philosophical Society that what is called hypnotism in the West is only a part of the real thing, and that the Hindus call it self-hypnotisation.[2] I explained that the great danger of psychic powers is that man stumbles into them without training and without knowledge of what has happened to him.[3] I argued that every other religion that preaches these things as real is practicing a form of hypnotism, and that the Advaitist alone does not care to be hypnotised.[2] I stated that the study of higher psychology has been retarded by its being identified with mere alleged psychic phenomena, as is done by some mystery-mongering order of Hindu fakirs.[4] I said that if there is no heaven, there is no earth; and if there is no God, there is no man, and that you are under this hypnotism as long as you are under it, you will have to see God and nature and the soul.[5] I emphasized that every man can say this theory is right, but that is not realization; he must realize it, and that will be when the hypnotism will break — even for a moment.[6]

question: What did you tell the Alambazar Math members about rules of the monastery?

result.text: I wrote to the members of the Alambazar Math from High View on April 27, 1896, emphasizing the importance of following rules for the well-being of the world.[1] I explained that it is necessary at the immature stage to be guided by rules, just as the Master used to say that the sapling must be hedged round.[1] I warned against feelings of jealousy or egotism gaining ground among them, as it would be a great pity if such feelings were to develop.[1] I also mentioned that it is natural for idle minds to indulge in gossip and faction-mongering, and hence I provided some hints for them to follow.[1] I encouraged them to contribute to the great well-being of the world, though most of them may not yet be aware of it.[1]

question: What did you say about Mahavira and Indian history?

result.text: I spoke about Mahavira in a conversation with Sharat Chandra Chakravarty, where I emphasized the importance of making Mahavira's character your ideal.[1] I described Mahavira as a perfect master of his senses and wonderfully sagacious, someone who had no care for life or death.[1] I urged people to build their lives on the great ideal of personal service, which Mahavira exemplified.[1] I mentioned that through such whole-hearted devotion, all other ideals would gradually manifest in life.[1] I also spoke about the need to revive the austere spirit of heroic manhood in India, which Mahavira represented.[1]

question: What did you write about the East and the West in your essay?

result.text: I wrote that the East and the West are both good, and neither can be praised nor blamed more than the other, as both scales are equal.[1] I noted that in the West, ideas of decency and etiquette vary according to the different countries, with the English and Americans having one type, the French another, and the Germans yet another.[2] I observed that the East and the West have different ideals, with the East focusing on producing perfect individuals through Sannyasa and concentration, while the West aims at perfecting the social state.[3] I mentioned that there is more chance of working out my plans in the East than in the West, as it now appears.[4] I suggested that the future may hold the conjunction of the East and the West, a combination which would be productive of marvellous results.[5]

question: What did you say about Tantra and the Tantras?

result.text: As I told the audience at Dacca, I have no faith in the theories advanced by Western savants with regard to the Vedas.[1] I explained that the Puranas are authoritative only in so far as they agree with the Vedas, otherwise not.[1] I acknowledged that the Tantras contain many high and sublime Vedantic thoughts, and that they are not so bad as people are inclined to think.[1] I denounced only the present corrupted form of Vâmâchâra of the Tantras, not the Mother-worship or the real Vamachara.[2] I stated that the Tantras represent the Vedic rituals in a modified form, and that their Mantras are taken verbatim from the Brahmanas.[3] I emphasized that the Tantras, in vogue amongst us, were the creation of the Buddhists themselves, and that they are even more dreadful than our doctrine of Vâmâchâra.[4] I said that the days of practising the Tantra in that fashion are gone, and that the Vedas should be studied instead.[5] I noted that the Tantras, like the Puranas, attempt to revive the old sacrificial ideas of the Karma Kanda.[6]

question: What did you say about spiritualism and talking to the dead?

result.text: I wrote to the editor of Light that the truth of correspondence between the living and the dead is in every religion, and nowhere more than in the Vedantic sects of India, where the fact of mutual help between the departed and the living has been made the basis of the law of inheritance.[1] I told the audience at the lecture on Formal Worship that there was one of those ladies who bring the departed spirits down to us — a medium, and that the spirits were all very polite to me.[2] I remarked that I had attended several spiritualistic meetings, and in one, the leader was a woman who said to me, 'Your mother and grandfather came to me' and that they greeted her and talked to her.[3] I expressed my belief that people should be warned of their dangers, with love and sympathy, and that I would be very sorry if I were mistaken as antagonistic to any sect or form of religion, so far as they are sincere.[1] I stated that I had witnessed some cases of spiritualism, but they seemed to be a hoax, and that I would test some more before coming to a final conclusion.[4] I remarked that I would be very sorry to know that my dead father is still wearing his filthy body, and that people get consolation from the idea that their fathers are all encased in matter.[3] I wrote that Spiritualism could not have played any part in the development of the God of the Jews, because how could the man who did not believe in any soul after death have anything to do with Spiritualism?[5]

question: What did you say about the poverty of your own family?

result.text: I wrote to Maharaja Ajit Singh that after trying a different climate for two years, I was getting worse every day and now almost at death's door.[1] I told him that I had one great sin rankling always in my breast, and that was neglecting my mother in order to do a service to the world.[1] I mentioned that since my second brother had gone away, my mother had become awfully worn-out with grief.[1] I expressed my desire to make Sevâ and serve my mother for some years at least, and to live with her and get my younger brother married to prevent the extinction of the family.[1] I wrote to Marie Halboister that the greatest misery in my life has been my own people — my brothers and sisters and mother.[2] I told her that relatives are like deadly clogs to one's progress, and it is a wonder that people still go on to find new ones by marriage.[2] In a letter to Miss Mary Hale, I described how my life was made up of continuous blows, and how poverty, treachery, and my own foolishness had caused me great suffering.[3]

question: What did you say about the Chicago Fair and your early days in America?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from Breezy Meadows on August 20, 1893, that I reached Vancouver from Japan and then went through Canada to Chicago, where I remained about twelve days and visited the Fair almost every day.[1] I told Alasinga that the Chicago Fair was a tremendous affair, requiring at least ten days to go through, and that I was warmly received by a member of the highest Chicago society.[1] I mentioned to Alasinga that in Chicago, a funny thing happened when the Raja of Kapurthala was being lionised by some portion of Chicago society, and an eccentric Mahratta Brahmin made false statements about him, which were picked up by the newspapers and led to the Raja being discredited.[2] I wrote to Alasinga that the American people have proved most interested audiences and sympathetic friends, and my work there has so taken root that I must shortly return to that country.[3] I told Alasinga that the American women are the most advanced in the world, far more cultivated than the average American man, and that they are kind-hearted and frank people.[4]

question: What did you say about your health and illness in your last years?

result.text: I wrote to Sister Christine from The Math on 1899-01-26 that I was once more in the vale of death, with the old diabetes having disappeared and replaced by asthma or dyspepsia due to nervous prostration.[1] I told Sister Christine from Ridgely Manor on 1899-10-30 that I was very anxious to know how she was and asked her to write a line to tell me she was in very good health.[2] In a letter to Sister Christine from The Math on 1898-10-25, I asked how she was and expressed my concern about her health, as I had not received any letters from her.[3] I wrote to Sister Christine from Suez on 1899-07-14 that I was so bad in health in India, with my heart going wrong due to mountain climbing, glacier water bathing, and nervous prostration, and that I had terrible asthma fits lasting about seven days and nights.[4] In a letter to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor on 1899-09, I mentioned that I had arrived and was writing a book on India and her people, and that I was going to learn French again to prepare for the Paris Exposition.[5] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from The Math on 1901-08-27 that my health was getting worse every day, with many complications and botherations, and that I had ceased to notice it at all.[6] In a conversation with Sharat Chandra Chakravarty, it was noted that I had just returned from East Bengal and Assam and was ill, with my feet swollen, but I still wore my usual smiling face and affectionate look despite my condition.[7]

question: What did you say about music and art in India?

result.text: I spoke about how in India, music was developed to the full seven notes, even to half and quarter notes, ages ago.[1] I noted that India led in music, also in drama and sculpture, and that whatever is done now is merely an attempt at imitation.[1] I explained that in India, drama and music are themselves held to be religion, and that any song, if one's whole soul is in that song, one attains salvation.[2] I mentioned that the real music in India lies in Kirtana and Dhrupada, while the rest has been spoiled by being modulated according to the Islamic methods.[3] I observed that the Mohammedans took up the different Râgas and Râginis after coming into India, but they put such a stamp of their own colouring on the art of Tappa songs that all the science in music was destroyed.[3] I pointed out that in India, the art of the West and that of India differ in that the former has a pointed expression, while the latter has a rolling wave-like movement.[4] I emphasized that each nation has a characteristic of its own, and that in India, the ideal is the transcendent Reality beyond nature, which is expressed in art through the powers of nature.[4] I noted that the music of the Westerners is much advanced, with the sentiment of pathos as well as of heroism in their music, which is as it should be.[5]

question: What is Karma-Yoga?

result.text:
In Karma-Yoga I set it down thus.
“The grandest idea in the religion of the Vedanta is that we may reach the same goal by different paths; and these paths I have generalised into four, viz those of work, love, psychology, and knowledge. But you must, at the same time, remember that these divisions are not very marked and quite exclusive of each other. Each blends into the other. But according to the type which prevails, we name the divisions. It is not that you can find men who have no other faculty than that of work, nor that you can find men who are no more than devoted worshippers only, nor that there are men who have no more than mere knowledge. These divisions are made in accordance with the type or the tendency that may be seen to prevail in a man. We have found that, in the end, all these four paths converge and become one. All religions and all methods of work and worship lead us to one and the same goal.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character].

question: What is Raja-Yoga?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Raja-Yoga, in the chapter Preface.
“The subject of the present book is that form of Yoga known as Raja-Yoga. The aphorisms of Patanjali are the highest authority on Raja-Yoga, and form its textbook. The other philosophers, though occasionally differing from Patanjali in some philosophical points, have, as a rule, acceded to his method of practice a decided consent. The first part of this book comprises several lectures to classes delivered by the present writer in New York. The second part is a rather free translation of the aphorisms (Sutras) of Patanjali, with a running commentary. Effort has been made to avoid technicalities as far as possible, and to keep to the free and easy style of conversation. In the first part some simple and specific directions are given for the student who wants to practice, but all such are especially and earnestly reminded that, with few exceptions, Yoga can only be safely learnt by direct contact with a teacher. If these conversations succeed in awakening a desire for further information on the subject, the teacher will not be wanting.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 8: Raja-Yoga in Brief]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 1: Introductory].

question: What is Jnana-Yoga?

result.text:
Here is what I said on this when I spoke on The First Step Towards Jnana.
“The word Jnâna means knowledge. It is derived from the root Jnâ — to know — the same word from which your English word to know is derived. Jnana-Yoga is Yoga by means of knowledge. What is the object of the Jnana-Yoga? Freedom. Freedom from what? Freedom from our imperfections, freedom from the misery of life. Why are we miserable? We are miserable because we are bound. What is the bondage? The bondage is of nature. Who is it that binds us?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, Introduction to Jnana-Yoga]; [Vol 8, Lectures and Discourses, Jnana Yoga].

question: What is the secret of work?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Karma-Yoga.
“What is Karma-Yoga? The knowledge of the secret of work. We see that the whole universe is working. For what? For salvation, for liberty; from the atom to the highest being, working for the one end, liberty for the mind, for the body, for the spirit. All things are always trying to get freedom, flying away from bondage. The sun, the moon, the earth, the planets, all are trying to fly away from bondage. The centrifugal and the centripetal forces of nature are indeed typical of our universe. Instead of being knocked about in this universe, and after long delay and thrashing, getting to know things as they are, we learn from Karma-Yoga the secret of work, the method of work, the organising power of work. A vast mass of energy may be spent in vain if we do not know how to utilise it.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 3: The Secret of Work]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character].

question: What is duty?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Karma-Yoga, in the chapter What Is Duty?.
“It is necessary in the study of Karma-Yoga to know what duty is. If I have to do something I must first know that it is my duty, and then I can do it. The idea of duty again is different in different nations. The Mohammedan says what is written in his book, the Koran, is his duty; the Hindu says what is in the Vedas is his duty; and the Christian says what is in the Bible is his duty. We find that there are varied ideas of duty, differing according to different states in life, different historical periods and different nations. The term "duty", like every other universal abstract term, is impossible clearly to define; we can only get an idea of it by knowing its practical operations and results. When certain things occur before us, we have all a natural or trained impulse to act in a certain manner towards them; when this impulse comes, the mind begins to think about the situation. Sometimes it thinks that it is good to act in a particular manner under the given conditions; at other times it thinks that it is wrong to act in the same manner even in the very same circumstances. The ordinary idea of duty everywhere is that every good man follows the dictates of his conscience. But what is it that makes an act a duty?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 2: Each Is Great in His Own Place].

question: What is Maya?

result.text:
In Jnana-Yoga I set it down thus.
“Almost all of you have heard of the word Mâyâ. Generally it is used, though incorrectly, to denote illusion, or delusion, or some such thing. But the theory of Maya forms one of the pillars upon which the Vedanta rests; it is, therefore, necessary that it should be properly understood. I ask a little patience of you, for there is a great danger of its being misunderstood. The oldest idea of Maya that we find in Vedic literature is the sense of delusion; but then the real theory had not been reached. We find such passages as, "Indra through his Maya assumed various forms." Here it is true the word Maya means something like magic, and we find various other passages, always taking the same meaning. The word Maya then dropped out of sight altogether. But in the meantime the idea was developing. Later, the question was raised: "Why can't we know this secret of the universe?" And the answer given was very significant: "Because we talk in vain, and because we are satisfied with the things of the senses, and because we are running after desires; therefore, we, as it were, cover the Reality with a mist." Here the word Maya is not used at all, but we get the idea that the cause of our ignorance is a kind of mist that has come between us and the Truth.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 4: Maya and the Evolution of the Conception of God]; [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 5: Maya and Freedom].

question: What is Prana?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Raja-Yoga.
“Prânâyâma is not, as many think, something about breath; breath indeed has very little to do with it, if anything. Breathing is only one of the many exercises through which we get to the real Pranayama. Pranayama means the control of Prâna. According to the philosophers of India, the whole universe is composed of two materials, one of which they call Âkâsha. It is the omnipresent, all-penetrating existence. Everything that has form, everything that is the result of combination, is evolved out of this Akasha. It is the Akasha that becomes the air, that becomes the liquids, that becomes the solids; it is the Akasha that becomes the sun, the earth, the moon, the stars, the comets; it is the Akasha that becomes the human body, the animal body, the plants, every form that we see, everything that can be sensed, everything that exists. It cannot be perceived; it is so subtle that it is beyond all ordinary perception; it can only be seen when it has become gross, has taken form. At the beginning of creation there is only this Akasha.” [1]

question: How should I practise meditation?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can guide you based on my teachings. Meditation should be of a negative nature, where you think away everything and analyse all thoughts by the sheer action of the will [1]. It is the one thing that brings you closest to spiritual life, where the mind meditates, and the Soul thinks of itself, free from all matter [2]. Meditation means turning the mind back upon itself, stopping all thought-waves, and allowing your consciousness to expand [3]. You may begin with an external object, such as a black point or a divine image, but eventually, you must reach a state where the mind is functionless, absorbed in the object of meditation [4]. Practise meditation with the utmost care, using external aids like fragrant flowers and incense to purify the mind at the outset [5]. Do not leave out a single day, and even if you have pressing work, dedicate at least a quarter of an hour to spiritual exercises [5]. Through consistent practice, meditation will bring you the most beautiful rest you ever had in your life [3].

question: What is Pratyahara?

result.text:
In Raja-Yoga I set it down thus.
“He who has succeeded in attaching or detaching his mind to or from the centres at will has succeeded in Pratyahara, which means, "gathering towards," checking the outgoing powers of the mind, freeing it from the thraldom of the senses. When we can do this, we shall really possess character; then alone we shall have taken a long step towards freedom; before that we are mere machines.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 8: Raja-Yoga in Brief]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Patanjali's Yoga Aphorisms].

question: What is the Atman?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Jnana-Yoga, in the chapter Ch. 14: The Atman: Its Bondage and Freedom.
“According to the Advaita philosophy, there is only one thing real in the universe, which it calls Brahman; everything else is unreal, manifested and manufactured out of Brahman by the power of Mâyâ. To reach back to that Brahman is our goal. We are, each one of us, that Brahman, that Reality, plus this Maya. If we can get rid of this Maya or ignorance, then we become what we really are. According to this philosophy, each man consists of three parts — the body, the internal organ or the mind, and behind that, what is called the Âtman, the Self. The body is the external coating and the mind is the internal coating of the Atman who is the real perceiver, the real enjoyer, the being in the body who is working the body by means of the internal organ or the mind.” [1]

question: What is the real nature of man?

result.text:
In Jnana-Yoga I set it down thus.
“We are not individuals yet. We are struggling towards individuality, and that is the Infinite, that is the real nature of man. He alone lives whose life is in the whole universe, and the more we concentrate our lives on limited things, the faster we go towards death. Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living. When he can say, "I am in everything, in everybody, I am in all lives, I am the universe," then alone comes the state of fearlessness. To talk of immortality in constantly changing things is absurd. Says an old Sanskrit philosopher: It is only the Spirit that is the individual, because it is infinite. No infinity can be divided; infinity cannot be broken into pieces. It is the same one, undivided unit for ever, and this is the individual man, the Real Man. The apparent man is merely a struggle to express, to manifest this individuality which is beyond; and evolution is not in the Spirit. These changes which are going on — the wicked becoming good, the animal becoming man, take them in whatever way you like — are not in the Spirit. They are evolution of nature and manifestation of Spirit.” [1]

question: What is the ideal of a universal religion?

result.text:
I spoke to this in my lecture The Ideal of a Universal Religion, in 1900.
“This is the existing condition of religion, the existing condition of things. What I want to propagate is a religion that will be equally acceptable to all minds; it must be equally philosophic, equally emotional, equally mystic, and equally conducive to action. If professors from the colleges come, scientific men and physicists, they will court reason. Let them have it as much as they want. There will be a point beyond which they will think they cannot go, without breaking with reason. They will say, "These ideas of God and salvation are superstitious, guise them up! " I say, "Mr. Philosopher, this body of yours is a bigger superstition. Give it up, don't go home to dinner or to your philosophic chair. Give up the body, and if you cannot, cry quarter and sit down." For religion must be able to show how to realise the philosophy that teaches us that this world is one, that there is but one Existence in the universe. Similarly, if the mystic comes, we must welcome him, be ready to give him the science of mental analysis, and practically demonstrate it before him. And if emotional people come, we must sit, laugh, and weep with them in the name of the Lord; we must "drink the cup of love and become mad". If the energetic worker comes, we must work with him, with all the energy that we have.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion].

question: What is the difference between religion and the religions?

result.text:
Here is what I said on this when I spoke on The Methods and Purpose of Religion.
“In studying the religions of the world we generally find two methods of procedure. The one is from God to man. That is to say, we have the Semitic group of religions in which the idea of God comes almost from the very first, and, strangely enough, without any idea of soul. It was very remarkable amongst the ancient Hebrews that, until very recent periods in their history, they never evolved any idea of a human soul. Man was composed of certain mind and material particles, and that was all. With death everything ended. But, on the other hand, there was a most wonderful idea of God evolved by the same race. This is one of the methods of procedure. The other is through man to God. The second is peculiarly Aryan, and the first is peculiarly Semitic.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy and Christianity]; [Vol 3, Lectures and Discourses, Unity, the Goal of Religion].

question: What is renunciation?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Raja-Yoga, in the chapter Patanjali's Yoga Aphorisms.
“The two motive powers of our actions are (1) what we see ourselves, (2) the experience of others. These two forces throw the mind, the lake, into various waves. Renunciation is the power of battling against these forces and holding the mind in check. Their renunciation is what see want. I am passing through a street, and a man comes and takes away my watch. That is my own experience. I see it myself, and it immediately throws my Chitta into a wave, taking the form of anger. Allow not that to come. If you cannot prevent that, you are nothing; if you can, you have Vairâgya. Again, the experience of the worldly-minded teaches us that sense-enjoyments are the highest ideal. These are tremendous temptations. To deny them, and not allow the mind to come to a wave form with regard to them, is renunciation; to control the twofold motive powers arising from my own experience and from the experience of others, and thus prevent the Chitta from being governed by them, is Vairagya. These should be controlled by me, and not I by them.” [1]

question: What is Para-Bhakti?

result.text:
In Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion I set it down thus.
“The higher knowledge is thus clearly shown to be the knowledge of the Brahman; and the Devi-Bhâgavata gives us the following definition of the higher love (Para-Bhakti): "As oil poured from one vessel to another falls in an unbroken line, so, when the mind in an unbroken stream thinks of the Lord, we have what is called Para-Bhakti or supreme love." This kind of undisturbed and ever-steady direction of the mind and the heart to the Lord with an inseparable attachment is indeed the highest manifestation of man's love to God. All other forms of Bhakti are only preparatory to the attainment of this highest form thereof, viz the Para-Bhakti which is also known as the love that comes after attachment (Râgânugâ). When this supreme love once comes into the heart of man, his mind will continuously think of God and remember nothing else. He will give no room in himself to thoughts other than those of God, and his soul will be unconquerably pure and will alone break all the bonds of mind and matter and become serenely free. He alone can worship the Lord in his own heart; to him forms, symbols, books, and doctrines are all unnecessary and are incapable of proving serviceable in any way. It is not easy to love the Lord thus. Ordinarily human love is seen to flourish only in places where it is returned; where love is not returned for love, cold indifference is the natural result.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 1: The Preparatory Renunciation]; [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 2: The Bhakta's Renunciation Results from Love].

question: What is the need of a Guru?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Bhakti-Yoga, in the chapter Ch. 4: The Need of Guru.
“Every soul is destined to be perfect, and every being, in the end, will attain the state of perfection. Whatever we are now is the result of our acts and thoughts in the past; and whatever we shall be in the future will be the result of what we think end do now. But this, the shaping of our own destinies, does not preclude our receiving help from outside; nay, in the vast majority of cases such help is absolutely necessary. When it comes, the higher powers and possibilities of the soul are quickened, spiritual life is awakened, growth is animated, and man becomes holy and perfect in the end.” [1]

question: What does the Vedanta say about God?

result.text:
Here is what I said on this when I spoke on Is Vedanta the Future Religion?.
“What is the God of Vedanta? He is principle, not person. You and I are all Personal Gods. The absolute God of the universe, the creator, preserver, and destroyer of the universe, is impersonal principle. You and I, the cat, rat, devil, and ghost, all these are Its persons — all are Personal Gods. You want to worship Personal Gods. It is the worship of your own self. If you take my advice, you will never enter any church. Come out and go and wash off. Wash yourself again and again until you are cleansed of all the superstitions that have clung to you through the ages. Or, perhaps, you do not like to do so, since you do not wash yourself so often in this country — frequent washing is an Indian custom, not a custom of your society.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy]; [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy and Christianity].

question: What is the cause of evil in the world?

result.text:
In Jnana-Yoga I set it down thus.
“With all dualistic theories the first difficulty is, how is it possible that under the rule of a just and merciful God, the repository of an infinite number of good qualities, there can be so many evils in this world? This question arose in all dualistic religions, but the Hindus never invented a Satan as an answer to it. The Hindus with one accord laid the blame on man, and it was easy for them to do so. Why? Because, as I have just now told you, they did not believe that souls were created out of nothing We see in this life that we can shape and form our future every one of us, every day, is trying to shape the morrow; today we fix the fate of the morrow; tomorrow we shall fix the fate of the day after, and so on. It is quite logical that this reasoning can be pushed backward too. If by our own deeds we shape our destiny in the future why not apply the same rule to the past? If, in an infinite chain, a certain number of links are alternately repeated then, if one of these groups of links be explained, we can explain the whole chain. So, in this infinite length of time, if we can cut off one portion and explain that portion and understand it, then, if it be true that nature is uniform, the same explanation must apply to the whole chain of time.” [1]

question: What is freedom?

result.text:
This is from the notes taken of my talk Freedom of the Self.
“As we cannot know except through effects that we have eyes, so we cannot see the Self except by Its effects. It cannot be brought down to the low plane of sense-perception. It is the condition of everything in the universe, though Itself unconditioned. When we know that we are the Self, then we are free. The Self can never change. It cannot be acted on by a cause, because It is Itself the cause. It is self-caused. If we can find in ourself something that is not acted on by any cause, then we have known the Self.” [1]

question: What is the ideal of Karma-Yoga?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Karma-Yoga.
“The grandest idea in the religion of the Vedanta is that we may reach the same goal by different paths; and these paths I have generalised into four, viz those of work, love, psychology, and knowledge. But you must, at the same time, remember that these divisions are not very marked and quite exclusive of each other. Each blends into the other. But according to the type which prevails, we name the divisions. It is not that you can find men who have no other faculty than that of work, nor that you can find men who are no more than devoted worshippers only, nor that there are men who have no more than mere knowledge. These divisions are made in accordance with the type or the tendency that may be seen to prevail in a man. We have found that, in the end, all these four paths converge and become one. All religions and all methods of work and worship lead us to one and the same goal.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 2: Each Is Great in His Own Place].

question: What is the Sankhya cosmology?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Raja-Yoga.
“The system of Yoga is built entirely on the philosophy of the Sânkhyas, as I told you before, and here again I shall remind you of the cosmology of the Sankhya philosophy. According to the Sankhyas, nature is both the material and the efficient cause of the universe. In nature there are three sorts of materials, the Sattva, the Rajas, and the Tamas. The Tamas material is all that is dark, all that is ignorant and heavy. The Rajas is activity. The Sattva is calmness, light. Nature, before creation, is called by them Avyakta, undefined, or indiscrete; that is, in which there is no distinction of form or name, a state in which these three materials are held in perfect balance. Then the balance is disturbed, the three materials begin to mingle in various fashions, and the result is the universe. In every man, also, these three materials exist. When the Sattva material prevails, knowledge comes; when Rajas, activity; and when Tamas, darkness, lassitude, idleness, and ignorance. According to the Sankhya theory, the highest manifestation of nature, consisting of the three materials, is what they call Mahat or intelligence, universal intelligence, of which each human intellect is a part. In the Sankhya psychology there is a sharp distinction between Manas, the mind function, and the function of the Buddhi, intellect.” [1]
